extracted.intended_audience: readers interested in culture, comedy criticism, and sexual-assault issues (ThinkProgress audience)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for judging stand-up comedy that uses rape as subject matter, especially how performers respond to hecklers and the ethical/rhetorical implications of such jokes. Focus is an opinion-critique of a specific comedian's routine and conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Responding to hecklers
rubrics_metrics.description: A good comedian is an alchemist who can turn heckling into a transformative extended riff; a professional should be prepared to respond to heckling rather than simply doubling down.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The piece says: 'A good comedian is an alchemist who can turn heckling into a transformative extended riff.' It criticizes Tosh for 'just doubl[ing] down on the same points he was making rather than actually responding, or providing an example of a rape joke that his heckler might find funny, undermining her objection.' Prepare a thoughtful reply or riff rather than restating the same point; be ready for club-level heckling and use it constructively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punching up vs. punching down (target matters)
rubrics_metrics.description: Jokes that mock perpetrators can be defensible and 'very funny'; jokes that target victims or use victim imagery to elicit laughs are problematic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author notes: 'I think there is a case to be made that rape jokes that make fun of perpetrators can be very funny. Tosh didn’t go there, though.' Examples of routines are given where rape is used as a punchline about victims (e.g., sister/pepper-spray silly string routine, 'Acme Rape Trap'), implying those are less defensible. Aim your target at perpetrators or structures of harm rather than at victims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid trivializing or weaponizing sexual violence
rubrics_metrics.description: Using an image of a person being raped to mock or intimidate treats sexual violence as trivial and turns it into a rhetorical or literal weapon against audience members.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The post criticizes Tosh: 'in using an image of her getting raped to mock and intimidate her, kind of made her point instead of his own.' It also asserts: 'If rape was just hilarious and uproarious and trivial, it wouldn’t be a very effective rhetorical or literal weapon.' Do not employ depictions of sexual violence as a means to silence, intimidate, or score cheap rhetorical points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect audience members' values and boundaries
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedians should not tell audience members how they should feel about profoundly damaging subjects; dismissing an expressed objection is uncivil and inappropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The heckler said, 'Actually, rape jokes are never funny!' The piece emphasizes that the heckler acted from 'values as a person and as a woman' and criticizes Tosh for effectively telling her she should find such jokes funny. Respect expressed objections rather than insisting people must accept your framing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid repetitive, lazy material; strive for thoughtful, analytical humor
rubrics_metrics.description: Repetitive statements that a certain category of jokes 'is always funny' are lazy; better material is thoughtful or analytical about the subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author observes: 'So Tosh then starts making some very generalizing, declarative statements about rape jokes always being funny... I don’t know why he was so repetitive about it' and calls some of his routines 'not particularly thoughtful or analytical.' Avoid repetition and take time to craft nuance rather than relying on slogans or shock alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professional preparedness for club dynamics
rubrics_metrics.description: Comics working in club settings should anticipate and be prepared for heckling and the particular dynamics of smaller venues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The post notes heckling 'does happen during comedy performances (though more so in clubs like the Laugh Factory than in a major auditorium)' and adds: 'a professional should have been prepared to respond to them.' Be situationally aware and have strategies for handling disruption without resorting to intimidation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not use humor to silence dissent
rubrics_metrics.description: Using jokes or violent imagery to 'run' a dissenting audience member out of the venue is unethical and bad craft.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author states Tosh 'took the quickest route to run his heckler out of the club' by invoking an image of her being raped. This is characterized as failing civility and as 'being a bad comedian.' Comedy should not be deployed primarily as a tool to silence or intimidate critics in the room.
